By default the app follows your phone\'s language. Change it here if you want it different.
A dump does not say which model it is, so pick the profile here. Each device keeps its own save data.
A faster game clock makes your Tama age faster. Animations and sound stay at normal speed. Steps: 1 2 5 10 30 60 120 300 600.

On by default, and best left that way. The real device blanks its screen after a few seconds, and while it sleeps its clock runs noticeably fast in the emulator \u2013 measured at about 1.5x. Turn this off only if you want the sleeping behaviour and can live with the clock drifting.

A call is recognised by its melody, so the SOUND INSIDE THE TAMAGOTCHI MUST STAY ON \u2013 check the sound setting in the device\'s own menu. If you do not want to hear it, turn off \"Sound\" here in the app instead: that only mutes the speaker, while vibration and the notification keep working.\n\nPressing any button counts as caring for your Tama and clears the call; an unanswered call expires by itself.

If the app was closed, the game clock afterwards runs faster until the missed time has been lived through. This makes up for lost GAME TIME so your Tama ages correctly \u2013 it does not set the clock to the phone\'s time of day. For that, use \"Set clock to phone time\" under Save data. Capped at 24 hours.
Set your Tama\'s clock to %s? Unlike catching up lost time, this is a jump \u2013 your Tama does not live through the skipped minutes.
Your Tama keeps its own clock, set when it hatched. It never follows the phone by itself. Use this if the two have drifted apart and you want them to match.
Start over? Like removing and reinserting the battery \u2013 your save data stays.
Runs the firmware from its boot screen again. Your save data is untouched.
Really delete the save data? Your Tama starts over.

Choose files (.jpg or .bin) made for exactly this device. For a multi part set, select all parts at once. A .bak copy is written before anything changes.\n\nSlots are few and fixed \u2013 a Tamagotchi iD L holds only TWO downloaded games. Built in games live elsewhere, so deleting one frees nothing. Free a slot above first.
emulator connected \u2013 waiting for the other phone
Put both phones on the same Wi-Fi. One phone hosts, the other connects to its address. Then open the connection screen on your Tama as usual.\nThis phone: %1$s, port %2$d
A trade off. Too little and Wi-Fi jitter corrupts bytes; too much and the firmware\'s own timeouts expire even though every byte arrives. If a visit fails, try the smallest value first.
Save data is written, then everything stops: emulator, background service and notifications. You start the app again yourself.
Stronger than restarting the emulator: nothing keeps running afterwards.

TamaEmu for Android %s

An Android port of tamaemu, an emulator for the colour Tamagotchi models built around the Epson S1C33 processor.

The emulator core was written by maragotchi:
https://github.com/maragotchi/tamaemu

This app is free software under the GNU General Public License version 3. That covers the emulator core and this port alike. The full licence text ships with the source code.

Source code for this app:
https://github.com/mameise/TamaEmu_Android

No firmware is included and none is ever uploaded. You need a ROM dump of a device you own; it is copied into the app's private folder and stays on your phone.
Emulation speed: %d %% of real time \u2013 this phone cannot quite keep up, so your Tama moves slower than the real device. Its clock still keeps the right time.

TamaEmu, plain \u2013 screen and buttons only
That file could not be read as an image.

You can replace the egg with your own artwork. Save a template first - it marks the egg outline, the screen and the three buttons exactly where the app draws them - then paint your case around those marks and pick the finished image here. The screen keeps the same size and position as with the egg. Templates are square because the image is stretched to the widget, so other shapes will distort. PNG with transparency works.

Fullscreen drops the title and system bars and gives the screen the whole window. „Keep pixels sharp“ decides how it is scaled: on, every emulated pixel stays the same size, which is crisp but leaves a border; off, the picture fills the area, which is much larger on a handheld but makes some pixels a touch wider than others. It stays square either way, so nothing is ever distorted.
